prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Imagine that you want to agree on a secret number with a friend you have never met, and the only way to talk to them is a line that anyone can listen to. At first this sounds impossible, because any message you send to set up the secret will be heard by the eavesdropper as well. For most of history, people who wanted to send secret messages first had to meet in private and swap a key, which was a shared code that both could use to lock and unlock their words. Public-key cryptography is the surprising idea that two strangers can build such a key out in the open, in full view of a listener, and still end up with something the listener cannot work out.

The trick rests on a particular kind of task, one that is easy to do in one direction and extremely hard to undo. Think of mixing paint. If you stir a spoonful of yellow into a pot of blue you get green very quickly, but nobody can look at a pot of green and separate it back into the exact yellow and blue you began with. Now imagine that you and your friend agree on a shared starting colour in public, and each of you secretly adds a private colour of your own. You swap the mixed pots across the open line, and each of you then adds your own private colour to the pot you received. Because the order of mixing does not matter, you both finish with the same final shade, while the eavesdropper, who saw only the starting colour and the two half-mixed pots, cannot reproduce it without unmixing paint. Mathematics lets us do this with numbers instead of paint.

The numbers we need come from something you already know, which is clock arithmetic. On a clock with twelve hours, if it is ten o'clock and you wait five hours, you do not get fifteen o'clock, you get three, because we wrap around once we pass the top. Mathematicians call this working modulo twelve, and the same idea works for a clock with any number of positions. We will use a clock with twenty-three positions, numbered from zero to twenty-two, and whenever a calculation gives an answer larger than twenty-two, we divide by twenty-three and keep only the remainder. So thirty becomes seven, and a hundred becomes eight, since twenty-three goes into a hundred four times with eight left over. The fact that this wrapping scrambles numbers is exactly what makes it useful.

Here is the recipe. You and your friend, whom we will call Alice and Bob, publicly agree on two numbers, which are the size of the clock, twenty-three, and a base number, five. Anyone may know these. Alice then secretly chooses a private number, say six, and Bob secretly chooses his own, say fifteen. Alice multiplies five by itself six times, wraps the result around the clock, and gets eight, because five to the power six is 15,625, and that leaves a remainder of eight when divided by twenty-three. She sends this eight to Bob across the open line. Bob does the same with his private number, multiplying five by itself fifteen times and wrapping, which gives nineteen, and he sends the nineteen to Alice. Both of these numbers are public, like the half-mixed pots of paint.

Now comes the clever step. Alice takes the nineteen that Bob sent and multiplies it by itself six times, which is her own secret number, wrapping around the clock at the end. The result is two. Bob takes the eight that Alice sent and multiplies it by itself fifteen times, which is his secret number, and the result is also two. They have arrived at the same number without ever sending it. The reason is that each of them has effectively multiplied five by itself six times fifteen, which is ninety times, and it makes no difference whether you do the six first and the fifteen second or the other way round. That shared two is now their secret key, and it was never spoken aloud.

You might ask what stops the eavesdropper from doing the same. The listener knows the clock size, the base, and the two numbers eight and nineteen that crossed the line. What they lack is either private number, and to get one they would have to work out how many times five must be multiplied by itself to land on eight. With a clock as small as ours this is easy, since you can simply try every possibility in a few seconds, and you may well have spotted the answer already. This is why the example is only a toy. The security comes entirely from making the clock enormous, and that is where the one-way nature of the problem begins to bite.

Real systems use clocks with hundreds of digits rather than two. Raising a number to a huge power and wrapping it around such a clock can be done by a computer in a fraction of a second, because there are clever shortcuts that avoid multiplying a billion billion times. Going backwards, however, from the final answer to the number of multiplications, has no known shortcut, because the wrapping scrambles the answers so thoroughly that they look random and give no hint of how close you are. The only known approach is essentially to guess, and with a clock this large the number of guesses would exceed what all the computers on Earth could manage in the lifetime of the universe. The honest caveat is that nobody has proved that no shortcut exists, only that decades of effort by very clever people have failed to find one, and that is the basis of the trust we place in it.

The method we have described is known as Diffie-Hellman key exchange, named after the two researchers who published it in 1976. Other schemes, such as RSA, reach the same goal in a different way, using a public padlock that anyone can snap shut but only its owner can open. In both cases the feature that matters is the same, which is that part of the information can be made public and part must stay private, and the link between them runs in one direction only. This is what puts the word public in the name, since the numbers you shout across the open line are the public half of the arrangement.

In practice, the shared number is not used to hide messages directly. It is fed into a much faster ordinary lock, in which both sides use the same key to scramble and unscramble everything they send afterwards. This is what your phone or computer does when you see the little padlock in a web browser, and it happens in a blink with a server you have never encountered before. The public-key step is only the introduction that lets two strangers agree on a key, after which the faster lock takes over for the conversation itself.

There is one remaining danger, which is that the exchange protects you from a listener but not from an impostor. If someone sits in the middle of the line and pretends to be Bob to Alice, and Alice to Bob, they can run two separate exchanges and read everything as it passes through. To defeat this, real systems add a way of checking identity, usually a certificate that a trusted authority has signed to say that a particular public number really belongs to a particular person or website. Together, the one-way mathematics and the identity check are what let strangers on a crowded network share secrets safely.
